title: Proton transfer reactions
summary: Brønsted–Lowry acids donate protons and bases accept them. Identify conjugate pairs, use pH and Kw, and distinguish strong from weak acids; at HL, Ka, pKa, buffers, salt hydrolysis and pH curves.

keyterms.definition: A species that donates a proton (H⁺).
A species that accepts a proton (H⁺).
Two species differing by one proton, e.g. CH₃COOH / CH₃COO⁻.
Able to both donate and accept a proton, e.g. H₂O, HCO₃⁻.
pH = −log₁₀[H⁺]; a decrease of 1 pH unit means a tenfold increase in [H⁺].
Kw = [H⁺][OH⁻] = 1.00 × 10⁻¹⁴ at 298 K; increases with temperature.
An acid that dissociates (almost) completely in water, e.g. HCl, HNO₃, H₂SO₄.
An acid that only partially dissociates in water, e.g. CH₃COOH, H₂CO₃.
Reaction of an acid with a base to form a salt and water; exothermic.
Ka = [H⁺][A⁻]/[HA]; larger Ka (smaller pKa) means a stronger acid. pKa = −log Ka.
A solution that resists pH change when small amounts of acid or base are added; a weak acid and its conjugate base (or weak base and conjugate acid).
A weak acid whose conjugate forms differ in colour; chosen so its colour change (pKa ± 1) lies on the steep part of the pH curve.
Reaction of the ions of a salt with water, giving a non-neutral solution, e.g. CH₃COO⁻ makes sodium ethanoate solution basic.

questions.prompt: In NH₃ + H₂O ⇌ NH₄⁺ + OH⁻, which species acts as the Brønsted–Lowry acid?
questions.explanation: Water donates a proton to ammonia (forward reaction).

questions.text: The conjugate base of H₂SO₄ is ___.
questions.explanation: Remove one H⁺: H₂SO₄ → HSO₄⁻.
It can donate a proton (forming OH⁻) or accept one (forming H₃O⁺).

questions.prompt: What is the pH of 0.010 mol dm⁻³ HCl?
questions.explanation: HCl is strong, so [H⁺] = 0.010 = 10⁻²; pH = 2.

questions.text: At 298 K, [OH⁻] in a solution with [H⁺] = 1.0 × 10⁻³ mol dm⁻³ is 1.0 × 10⁻___ mol dm⁻³.

questions.prompt: Match each acid with its conjugate base.
questions.explanation: Each pair differs by one H⁺.

questions.statement: A solution of pH 3 has ten times the [H⁺] of a solution of pH 4.
questions.explanation: pH is logarithmic: one unit = factor of 10.

questions.prompt: 0.10 mol dm⁻³ solutions of HCl and CH₃COOH are compared. Which is true?
options: They need different volumes of NaOH to neutralize
questions.explanation: HCl is fully dissociated, so [H⁺] is higher; both need the same NaOH because the total amount of acid is the same.

questions.prompt: Order these 0.1 mol dm⁻³ solutions by pH, lowest first.
questions.explanation: Strong acid < weak acid < neutral salt < weak base < strong base.

questions.prompt: Which is a product of neutralizing sulfuric acid with potassium hydroxide?
questions.explanation: H₂SO₄ + 2KOH → K₂SO₄ + 2H₂O.

lessons.title: Reactions of acids and pH changes

questions.prompt: Which gas is produced when an acid reacts with a carbonate?
questions.explanation: Acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide.
Hydroxides are bases; neutralization forms a salt and water.

questions.statement: Reactive metals such as magnesium react with dilute acids to give hydrogen gas.
questions.explanation: e.g. Mg + 2HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂.

questions.prompt: What is the pH of 0.0010 mol dm⁻³ NaOH at 298 K?
Match each reaction to its products.
questions.explanation: NH₃ + HCl → NH₄Cl: no water forms.
Water dissociation is endothermic, so Kw increases with temperature; pure water at 50 °C has pH below 7 but is still neutral.

questions.prompt: A strong acid is titrated with a strong base. The pH at the equivalence point is…
questions.explanation: The salt of a strong acid and strong base (e.g. NaCl) gives a neutral solution.

questions.text: A 100-fold dilution of a strong acid raises its pH by ___ units.
questions.explanation: [H⁺] falls by 10², so pH rises by 2.

questions.prompt: Order the pH readings as NaOH is gradually added to HCl in a flask.
items: Slow rise while acid is in excess
Sharp jump near the equivalence point
Levels off near 13 with excess base
questions.explanation: The steep vertical section is where indicators change colour.
Carbonic acid only partially dissociates; the others are strong.
Smaller pKa means larger Ka, a stronger acid.

questions.text: For a weak acid at 298 K, pKa + pKb (of its conjugate base) = ___.
questions.explanation: Ka × Kb = Kw, so pKa + pKb = pKw = 14.

questions.prompt: [H⁺] in 0.10 mol dm⁻³ HA (Ka = 1.0 × 10⁻⁵) is approximately…

questions.statement: A mixture of ethanoic acid and sodium ethanoate acts as a buffer.
questions.explanation: CH₃COO⁻ removes added H⁺; CH₃COOH neutralizes added OH⁻.

questions.text: At the half-equivalence point of a weak acid–strong base titration, pH = ___.
questions.explanation: Half the acid has been converted to A⁻, so [HA] = [A⁻] and [H⁺] = Ka.

questions.prompt: Match each salt solution to its pH.
questions.explanation: Ions from weak acids or bases react with water (hydrolysis).

questions.prompt: Which indicator suits a weak acid–strong base titration (equivalence pH ≈ 9)?
questions.explanation: The indicator range must fall on the steep part, which lies above pH 7 here.

questions.statement: Adding a small amount of strong acid to a buffer leaves its pH completely unchanged.
questions.explanation: Buffers resist change: the pH changes only slightly, because the added H⁺ is mostly removed by the conjugate base.

questions.prompt: Order the regions of a weak acid–strong base pH curve.
questions.explanation: The buffer region is flattest around the half-equivalence point.

questions.prompt: Which pair could form a basic buffer?
questions.explanation: A weak base with its conjugate acid buffers around pH 9.
